The gate is the courthouse, and they explain the arrangement rather than assume it. Gill puts the hour at midday on Josephus's authority and notes that the gate is where traffic to and from the country passes and where judgment was given, the Targum calling it the gate of the house of judgment. Ellicott accounts for the going up by the lie of the ground, the town standing on a hill where Ruth had been told the night before to go down to the threshing-floor. Clarke sets out the procedure in eight steps — the plaintiff waits at the gate, stops the other man as he passes to work, calls him by name, ten elders are seated, the suit is stated, the answer returned, judgment given by the custom of the place, and whoever is present serves as witness — then turns it against his own age, saying such a question in a modern court would take days of preparation and hours of argument between two counsel before an honest judge could decide whether Naomi might sell her own land. Gill and Wesley agree on why ten were called: two or three witnesses sufficed in ordinary matters, but ten was the settled number in causes of marriage and transferred inheritance, the elders being judges and witnesses at once.

Henry asks what none of the others do, why Boaz should be in such haste over the match. Ruth was not rich but lived on alms, not honourable but a poor stranger, and is nowhere called beautiful — if she ever had been, he says, weeping and travelling and gleaning had withered her lilies and roses. What made Boaz eager was the one thing all her neighbours agreed on, that she was a virtuous woman, which set her price with him far above rubies. Henry also defends his dignity, since being found asleep the night before at the end of a heap of corn was no bar, in those days of plainness, to sitting as judge in the gate next morning. On the way the other kinsman is hailed, Clarke renders the two Hebrew words as so-and-so of such a place and derives them from roots meaning to hide and to distinguish, noting that the Greek turned the first into a word for an unknown person. Ellicott takes the same derivation and draws the paradox out, one pointed at and concealed in the same breath.

Why the name is withheld is left open. Ellicott offers two possibilities, that the writer did not know it or judged it unworthy of record since the man failed his plain duty, and adds what the failure cost him, an offer carrying the glory of being ancestor to the Christ born in the far-off ages. On the sale Ellicott corrects the English tense: the land had already been sold, so far as an Israelite could part with a family estate, and Boaz proposes to redeem it at once rather than wait for the jubilee — much as the owner of a freehold might buy out the residue of a lease to occupy his own ground. Clarke explains the necessity, that she was reduced to want and the immediate heirs extinct. Wesley catches the tactics: both women had an interest for their lives, yet only Naomi is named, lest mentioning Ruth should suggest that marrying her was part of the bargain before the man had answered the first proposal. That is how it works out, since Clarke observes he did not know of the condition and Ellicott that he was willing enough to take the land as an investment, forgetting until reminded what came with it. Clarke and Ellicott both note that the manuscripts correct a pronoun here, and Ellicott prefers those sitting to those dwelling, where Keil reports that many read it of the townspeople and then declines to follow them.
5:
Gill says outright that the condition had been kept back on purpose, to try whether the man would hold to his answer once he heard the whole of it. Clarke sharpens the rendering, that the buyer does not so much purchase Ruth as acquire her, the land being unobtainable without her, and that any children would be reckoned to the dead man. Ellicott sets out the layers of claim in order — the purchaser bought out first, then Naomi's own right, then Ruth's as widow of Elimelech's son — and shows why the last of them changes everything, since a child had to be born who could inherit as Mahlon's son. Wesley refers the whole arrangement to the law of the surviving brother and glosses the purpose in a phrase, to revive a name that was buried with the body.

Why the man drew back is answered two ways. Keil works it as arithmetic: redemption had to be paid for, since the produce of the field until the jubilee was part of the price, and if he took the land outright his own holding grew by that much — but marry Ruth and the field would pass to her son, so he would have laid out capital and reduced his own estate to buy an inheritance for somebody else. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion and compares it to mortgaging one's own land for another man's benefit. The rival explanation is domestic and comes from the ancient versions: he had a wife already, and a second would bring contention into the house. Gill reports it and adds from Josephus that there were children too; Clarke quotes it at length and then refuses it, saying the gloss has no foundation in the law of Moses. Wesley offers a third possibility alongside the first, that a man with children already would see a small gain divided among many heirs.

The shoe divides them further. Gill argues that what is described is a custom and not a statute, since neither of the two laws usually cited fits — one concerns redemption by a kinsman but prescribes no such rite, the other concerns a brother rather than a kinsman and its ceremony on refusal is quite different — though he notes that Josephus is express that the law is meant, and that a Jewish commentator extends the practice to the exchange of one field for another. Clarke agrees the fuller ceremony is not in use here and explains the difference: in the law the widow pulled off the shoe and spat in the man's face, and he was disgraced ever after, whereas here only the shoe comes off, the man having a reasonable excuse, so the contemptuous half is dropped. Keil traces the symbol to the taking of land by treading on it, notes the same practice among the Indians and the old Germans, and argues from the words in former time that the usage had lapsed before the book was written. Ellicott resists that inference, since the phrase is used elsewhere of no great antiquity, and reads the act simply as resigning the right to walk the ground as master.
9:
Henry reads the transaction as a use of money rather than a display of it, since only a man of substance could have compassed the redemption at all, and asks what a great estate is good for except that it lets a man do so much the more good in his generation, particularly to his own household. He notes the commercial shape of it without flinching: there was no portion with her, what jointure she had was encumbered, and Boaz could not get it without paying its full worth, so he might well say he had purchased her — and being a virtuous woman, he reckoned the bargain a good one. Henry also draws a rule from the publicity, that the more openly estates are sold the better they are guarded against fraud. Clarke doubts any document was drawn up at all, thinking the appeal was simply made to those present and answered by them, and he sets out the sort of minute a court would have entered if it kept any. Keil sums up the conduct rather than the procedure, that Boaz acted as unselfishly as he acted honourably in upholding a laudable family custom.

Gill alone stops to ask whether the marriage was lawful, and answers it in three steps: Moab was not among the nations with which marriage was forbidden; Ruth had in any case become a proselyte, which meets the objection from her idolatrous people; and the standing prohibition is read by the Jewish authorities as binding men only, an Ammonite and a Moabite being barred perpetually while their women are free at once. The blessing that follows is measured out by the rest of them. Keil calls it the greatest blessing of marriage. Ellicott and Clarke both notice that the Hebrew for building yields the words for son and daughter, so that a family is raised as a house is; Clarke adds a line from a Roman comedy where parents are called the builders and the children the foundation. Ellicott presses further on the phrase rendered do thou worthily, whose noun means force or substance — the valour of a soldier, the resources of a country, and the quality named in the woman more precious than rubies — so that the wish for Boaz is that his own energy may keep him prosperous, and the next clause is literally to proclaim a name.

Why Rachel is named before Leah gets two answers. Ellicott suggests it is her burial near this very place, and makes that explain how a later prophet's words about Rachel weeping came to be applied where they were. Wesley gives the domestic reason instead, that she was the most lawful and best-beloved wife, and adds why the pair are chosen at all: both were of foreign stock yet grafted into the people, as Ruth was, and both were granted a fruitfulness beyond the two wives before them. The second half of the blessing looks back to another irregular birth. Gill observes that Pharez too was born of a woman from outside Israel, that his was one of the five families of Judah, and reports without endorsing the Jewish identification of Boaz with a judge said to have had thirty sons and thirty daughters, remarking only that it wants proof. Keil traces the line of Boaz himself back to Pharez, so the wish is that this house may grow as that one did. Ellicott finds the exact parallel in the manner of the birth, since Judah had unwittingly discharged the very obligation Boaz was now discharging on purpose, and the child born of it became heir to the eldest son and head of the house.
13:
Henry measures the marriage against the sister who turned back, and thinks Orpah, having returned to her people and her gods, was never half so well preferred; he adds that whoever forsakes all for Christ finds more than all with him, repaid a hundredfold in this present time, and Wesley closes his own note on the verse with the same sentence. Henry notices too that Boaz had prayed for a full reward on the woman who had come to trust under those wings, and now became himself the instrument of the answer, so that she had the command of the servants she had worked among and the fields she had gleaned in. On whether the marriage was permitted, Clarke grants the prohibition against Moabites to the tenth generation but reports the Jewish view that it did not reach women, and adds that hers might be an exempt case in any event, since she had already been taken into the family and had left her country, her people and her gods; Wesley reaches the same end more simply, restricting the ban to those who continue heathen. Gill observes that nothing was done beyond what the text records, the later ceremonies not yet being in use.

Who the redeemer is in the women's blessing divides them. Keil says plainly that it is not Boaz but the newborn child, and rejects the reading that would make him a redeemer of Naomi's property; he is her redeemer because as Ruth's son he is also hers, and will lift the reproach of childlessness, comfort her and keep her in her old age. Ellicott agrees in a line that the kinsman meant is the child. Wesley takes it the other way, rendering the clause as thanks that God had not suffered her kinsman to fail her, that is, to refuse his duty as the other kinsman had. On the daughter-in-law being worth more than seven sons, Keil explains the number as the measure of a family richly blessed, such a mother having both support in age and the prospect that her line would continue — and Naomi had something better still. Ellicott adds that the verb is a perfect and should read who has ever loved thee, and that the pronoun stands in an emphatic place. Wesley draws the lesson out: God sometimes makes up the want of those from whom we expected most comfort in those from whom we expected least, and the bonds of love prove stronger than those of nature.

Clarke turns the nursing into a medical warning and will not be hurried past it. It might do for Naomi, he says, but it was bad for the child, since the aged draw refreshment and energy from the young while the young take premature decrepitude in exchange; he calls it a foolish and destructive custom to let children sleep with aged relations, identifies this as the whole of Bacon's enigmatic secret for prolonging life, and explains on the same principle why physicians once recommended a young woman to sleep beside an aged king. Ellicott keeps to the word, noting that the verb is the one used where kings are called nursing fathers rather than the ordinary word for a woman. On the name, Gill reports that Josephus makes Naomi give it on the neighbours' advice, probably at the circumcision, and sets the Jewish practice beside the Roman and the Greek, which named on the eighth or ninth or tenth day; Wesley insists the women only advised, having no right to name a child themselves. Keil denies that the name means servant of the Lord and makes it simply the serving one, with reference to what the boy would be to his grandmother — and Clarke, having already decided what that service was, says the neighbours were skillful people.
18:
Both of the reasons for starting the list where it starts are given. Keil takes it as family history: the line is traced from Perez because he founded the branch of Judah that carries his name, and it was to that branch that Elimelech and Boaz belonged. Gill takes it as prophecy: the point of the list is to make good the old word that the ruler should come from Judah, so it begins with a son of Judah whom nobody disputes and ends with the king whose son the Messiah was to be. Clarke notices where the same ten names turn up again, with only trifling changes of form, in the opening of the first Gospel. Keil fills in what is known of the middle of the line and how little that is — Hezron counted among those who went down into Egypt though born there, Ram appearing as Aram in the Greek and so in the evangelist, Amminadab remembered as the father of the tribe-prince of Judah and as the father-in-law of Aaron, and of Ram himself nothing else recorded anywhere.

Ellicott stops on the arithmetic and finds it will not work. Taking the four hundred and eighty years given from the Exodus to the fourth year of Solomon, subtracting the forty in the wilderness and the seventy of David's life and the four of the reign, he is left with three hundred and sixty-six years between the entry into Canaan and David's birth; and if Salmon married Rahab early in that stretch, then Boaz, Obed and Jesse must cover almost the whole of it between them, each begetting his son past the age of a hundred. He judges that hardly credible and concludes instead that a link or two has dropped out, most likely before Boaz, so that what survives is the distinguished names with lesser ones passed over. Keil, counting the same generations, notices the same shortness. Ellicott also thinks Salmon may well have been one of the two spies whom Rahab hid, repaying her afterwards by marrying her, which is the tradition Gill states flatly when he says Boaz was her son.

Clarke gives most of his space to the Targum, which paraphrases these five verses at length, and he quotes the additions rather than summarising them. Salmon becomes Salmah the Just of Bethlehem and Netopha, whose sons pulled down the watches Jeroboam had set on the roads; Boaz becomes Boaz the Just, for whose righteousness Israel was delivered from its enemies and at whose prayer the famine left the land; Obed served the Lord in this world with a perfect heart. Jesse is given a second name and a strange reason for it, that no iniquity was found in him for which the angel of death might take him, so that he lived on until the counsel the serpent gave to Eve was remembered and he died by that guilt alone. Clarke calls this no small or indistinct reference to original sin and takes it as evidence of what the older rabbis held; he also records which printed editions carry these additions and which do not. On the spelling of one name he reports the conjecture that an early copyist mistook two letters for one before the final forms were settled, and Gill notes the same name standing three different ways in three places.
